# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Children increasingly read machine-generated stories on screens, and whether the text properties that govern reading in the laboratory also govern it there is unknown. We will analyse logs from *Let's Story*, a feature of the *Applaydu* app, in which children aged 7 and older read in ten or more languages. We will model reading time per word from lexical difficulty, grammatical load and referential continuity. Six confirmatory hypotheses concern these associations, their moderation by age band, narration's selectivity, children's difficulty ratings and accumulated in-app reading. Bayesian crossed-effects models will represent readings within texts, children and languages. Coefficients outside a region of practical equivalence would support the hypotheses, in either direction for the two that adjudicate between rival developmental accounts, and posteriors inside it would show that the laboratory effects do not transfer. Because families choose narration, texts and continued use, we will report every coefficient as a conditional association.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Introduction

A generation of children now does part of its reading on a screen, and some of what appears there was written by a machine. In the United Kingdom, one in five 8- to 18-year-olds read fiction on screen at least monthly in 2025, print fiction had fallen from three in five to one in two since 2017, and the children who read fiction only on screen were disproportionately those who enjoy reading least [@pictonTrendsChildrenYoung2026]. Commercial storytelling applications generate a narrative to order, read it aloud in the family's language, and record what the child did with it. One such feature reported 2.4 million story sessions in its first six months [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025], while many of the parents interviewed in one small study wanted the plot and dialogue of a child's story to remain human-authored, accepting machine-made illustrations only on that condition [@jinTheyAllLook2025]. The behavioural record such platforms accumulate is far larger than any laboratory corpus of children's reading, spans ten or more languages, and arises under exactly the conditions that laboratory work has to strip away. We ask whether the text properties that govern reading under controlled conditions still govern it outside the laboratory, and whether their hold on the reader changes over the years in which decoding becomes automatic. Whatever the answer, the estimate is one that no laboratory can supply, since it concerns how far three determinants of reading established under experimental control carry into unsupervised reading of generated stories, at scale, in ten languages, with the developmental change in each.

The laboratory answer is well established at three levels of linguistic description. At the level of the word, high-frequency words are recognised faster and fixated for less time than low-frequency words, and the effects of frequency and of word length on text reading are closely similar across 12 alphabetic languages [@kupermanWordLengthFrequency2024a]. Word-length effects take a script-specific form outside the Roman alphabet [@lahoudDevelopmentalStudyEye2023], and Korean is the one language in this sample to which that caution applies. Children's eye movements are driven by the frequency of the words they meet [@josephUsingEyeMovements2013], and where children were tested against adult controls, the length and frequency effects were the larger in the children [@tiffin-richardsWordLengthFrequency2015], the difference that an account on which the effect tracks accumulated exposure predicts [@brysbaertWordFrequencyEffect2018]. The same developmental pattern appears outside alphabetic scripts [@lianEffectsWordFrequency2026]. The Lexical Quality Hypothesis describes that difference [@perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007; @perfettiWordKnowledgeTheory2014]. A word is retrieved quickly and reliably in proportion to how well specified and tightly bound its orthographic, phonological and semantic constituents are, and that quality is built by reading itself [@nationNurturingLexicalLegacy2017; @castlesEndingReadingWars2018]. On that account, a text's lexical properties, the age band and a child's accumulated reading all bear on the cost of identifying a word, so Hypotheses 1 and 6 test it at different grains.

A second source of word-level cost is contextual. On surprisal theory, a word costs time in proportion to how unexpected it is given what precedes it [@haleProbabilisticEarleyParser2001; @levyExpectationbasedSyntacticComprehension2008]. The relation is close to linear in surprisal [@smithEffectWordPredictability2013; @shainLargescaleEvidenceLogarithmic2024] and holds in eleven languages from five families [@wilcoxTestingPredictionsSurprisal2023], and that linearity makes a text's mean per-word surprisal the natural text-level summary of the cost, which this design uses. Two qualifications are carried into the design. A text's overall difficulty moderates how strongly per-word surprisal bears on reading time, so the text-level mean is not a neutral summary of a constant word-level effect [@chenTextDifficultyModulates2026]. Frequency and surprisal are also hard to hold apart, since dissociable frequency effects shrink as surprisal predictors improve [@ohDissociableFrequencyEffects2025], which qualifies their reported additivity in naturalistic reading [@shainWordFrequencyPredictability2024]. A component that pools them indexes their joint contribution without resolving it, which is what the confirmatory claim asserts. How subword tokens are aggregated to words affects psycholinguistic estimates [@giulianelliProperTreatmentTokenization2024], and the unit over which surprisal should be defined is itself under revision [@kiegelandProperTreatmentUnits2026], so the aggregation rule is fixed under Materials. In children, contextual facilitation appears in the later eye-movement measures that a whole-text duration absorbs [@tiffinrichardsContextFacilitationText2020].

Further lexical properties are carried, each for a reason of its own. Concrete words are fixated for less time than abstract ones in natural reading, on every fixation measure where length and frequency were matched [@yaoEmotionProcessingConcrete2024] and on first-fixation duration where they were covaried instead [@magnaboscoEyeSemanticsStudy2024], an advantage usually traced to perceptual grounding on accounts that treat conceptual processing as partly modal and partly amodal [@kaupInterplayModalAmodal2025]. The age at which a word was learned bears on how quickly it is identified over and above how often it occurs [@juhaszAgeofacquisitionEffects2005]. Function words are skipped far more often than content words [@raynerEyeMovementsReading1998], so a text of higher lexical density, the proportion of tokens that are content words, presents more tokens that must be fixated and identified. Reading times for a word fall over repeated encounters, in children of 10 and 11 reading sentences [@josephExaminingIncidentalWord2018], so a lexical diversity index [@mccarthyMTLDVocdDHDD2010] tracks the share of tokens a reader meets for the first time. A word-level measure of informational cost predicts eye movements in first- and second-language readers of diverse writing systems [@kimchiQuantifyingWordInformativeness2025], though its authors test no text-level aggregate of the kind used here.

At the level of the sentence, structure imposes its own cost. Mean dependency distance indexes the distance over which a dependency has to be resolved, and clause density, subordination and noun-phrase depth index how many dependencies are open at once. That cost is not reducible to predictability. In 368 adults reading syntactically challenging sentences, language-model surprisal from 409 estimators approximated the early effects of disambiguation but not the additional rereading that repairing a structure incurred [@timkeyEyeMovementsReveal2026]. The grammatical features therefore form a family of their own and are never absorbed into surprisal. Gibson's [-@gibsonLinguisticComplexityLocality1998] theory separates the cost of keeping a prediction alive from the cost of integrating the element that completes it, and retrieval-based accounts place the cost at the point of resolution, where intervening and similar material slows retrieval [@lewisActivationbasedModelSentence2005]. Expectation-based accounts add that material before a head can make the head more predictable [@levyExpectationbasedSyntacticComprehension2008], so that in head-final configurations a longer dependency need not cost more. A clause-final verb has been read faster after longer intervening material in German and in Hindi [@koniecznyLocalityParsingComplexity2000; @vasishthArgumentheadDistanceProcessing2006], and the strength of a locality effect is expected to vary with a language's statistics [@futrellLossycontextSurprisalInformationtheoretic2020]. The grammatical slope is therefore allowed to vary by language in every model below.

Whether children bear these costs disproportionately is the question Hypothesis 2 takes up. Less settled is whether a grammatical cost appears at all at the grain this study uses. In naturalistic corpus reading by adults, a distance-based integration cost predicted reading times at nouns and at auxiliaries but not at words in general, whereas word predictability predicted them throughout [@dembergDataEyetrackingCorpora2008]. In the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus, global measures of syntactic and lexical complexity, among them the longest dependency path, the proportion of embedded sentences and mean sentence length, predicted adults' passage reading negligibly once passage length was accounted for, and at the sentence level only sentence length and position carried effects of any size [@kupermanGlobalMeasuresSyntactic2025]. That study's lexical measures proved as negligible as its syntactic ones, but its authors separate such global measures from the aggregate properties of the individual words a passage contains, and the lexical component here is anchored on those aggregates, mean frequency, word length and surprisal, whose word-level effects are well replicated across languages [@kupermanWordLengthFrequency2024a; @wilcoxTestingPredictionsSurprisal2023]. Whether a text-level grammatical measure carries a reading-time cost for children reading whole stories therefore remains open, and Hypothesis 1 is written so that either answer is informative.

At the level of the passage, what matters is whether the text states the connection between one idea and the next or leaves the reader to supply it. Sentence-to-sentence semantic similarity, overlap in referring expressions and the density of explicit connectives together index how much of that work the surface of the text has already done [@crossleyToolAutomaticAnalysis2019]. These are measures of cohesion, a property of the text, whereas coherence is a property of the representation the reader builds, and cohesion eases its construction without guaranteeing it [@mcnamaraCohMetrixCapturingLinguistic2010]. Referential overlap descends from the rule that connects propositions sharing an argument [@kintschModelTextComprehension1978], which the construction-integration model retains in the weights it assigns to propositions close together in the text base [@kintschRoleKnowledgeDiscourse1988], and semantic similarity between adjoining sentences approximates that propositional analysis [@foltzMeasurementTextualCoherence1998]. An explicit relational marker speeds processing of the segment it introduces without changing what is recalled [@sandersRoleCoherenceRelations2000]. Multi-dimensional characterisations of difficulty built from such indices outperform the classical readability formulae they replaced [@crossleyAssessingReadabilityFormulas2023]. Evaluated against eye movements, though, readability scorers account for real-time reading ease only partially [@grutekekleinEyeTrackingBased2026], which is one reason this study models the psycholinguistic features themselves and never a composite readability score.

The systematic review that accompanies this protocol sharpens that account in ways that shape the design, and Supplementary Section S2 tabulates the studies closest to it in method. Text difficulty does not reduce to word frequency: in German fourth-graders, estimated lexical coverage predicted comprehension non-linearly [@ludewigVocabularyTextCoverage2023]. In 158 children aged 8 to 11, word frequency, pronoun density, concreteness and deep cohesion each explained unique variance in passage comprehension after decoding and oral language were taken into account, and lexical arousal explained variance beyond them [@pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022], which warrants carrying affective and discourse variables alongside conventional readability measures. Syntactic complexity impaired comprehension accuracy and slowed recall in bilingual children [@wasitokiranaSentenceProcessingIndonesianEnglish2025]. In 5,133 second-graders reading informational text, word concreteness, referential cohesion and deep cohesion each predicted oral reading rate beyond the classical readability formulae [@tortorelliBeyondFirstGrade2020], and in first-graders a text-level vocabulary aggregate predicted rate, accuracy and comprehension [@brunerRoleTextVocabulary2026]. Both samples are younger than this study's bands and both read aloud, so they establish that text properties reach a rate measure without fixing the size of that reach for silent reading at 7 and over.

Two further strands concern the reader and the reading context. The first is the child's history of reading, which longitudinal work shows cannot be read as a simple dose of practice. In random-intercept cross-lagged models from ages 7 to 16, weaker early reading predicted less subsequent leisure reading, while later within-person increases in book reading predicted gains in comprehension [@torppaLeisureReadingNot2020]. A ten-year study likewise found reciprocal associations between skill and print exposure, with the skill-to-practice path most visible early and accumulated exposure more predictive later [@vanbergenHowArePractice2021]. Accumulated use of an app therefore carries both practice and the stable differences in skill and motivation that produced the use in the first place, which is why Hypothesis 6 separates within-child change from between-child differences. The setting matters as well as the quantity, since digital leisure reading and print reading do not relate to comprehension in the same way [@altamuraNewFormsReading2025] and digital leisure reading has an association with comprehension of its own, independent of print [@altamuraHowDigitalReading2025]. What Hypothesis 6 observes is reading inside one app.

The second is narration. Read-aloud audio is often treated as a uniform benefit, and the evidence does not support that reading. A meta-analysis of 30 reading-while-listening studies, 62 effects over a total *N* of 1,945, found a small pooled comprehension advantage ($g$ = 0.18). There was no reliable advantage where ordinary reading was self-paced ($g$ = 0.06, 95 per cent CI [-0.07, 0.19]), and a larger one only where ordinary reading was paced by the experimenter ($g$ = 0.41, 95 per cent CI [0.13, 0.70]) [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023]. Among students with reading difficulties, text-to-speech tools showed a moderate pooled effect ($d$ = 0.35) that fell to $d$ = 0.15 and included zero in within-participant designs [@woodUseTexttoSpeech2018]. Neither synthesis settles the mechanism, and a large naturalistic corpus is well placed to address it. A spoken rendition may work by supplying word identity, in which case it should remove much of the cost of lexical difficulty while leaving the cost of connecting ideas intact, or narrated reading time may simply be set by the duration of the recording. Hypothesis 4 is written to separate these accounts, and the mechanism of each is set out there.

The texts this platform serves are a population of stimuli produced by one process, and a process need not distribute text properties as human authorship does. Comparisons in other domains report that large-language-model output carries a distinct noun-heavy, informationally dense register even when prompted otherwise [@reinhartLLMsWriteHumans2025] and that human writing shows more scattered sentence-length distributions and more varied vocabulary than model output [@munoz-ortizContrastingLinguisticPatterns2024]. In creative writing, the domain closest to the stories read here, stylometric comparison separates the two on measurable features of style [@osullivanStylometricComparisonsHuman2025]. Whether the lexical, grammatical and discourse determinants established on human-written text describe reading across such a population is a question about the scope of that account [@haeffelTestsGeneralizabilityCan2022; @yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022], and the literature bearing on it can be counted.

On 26 August 2026, a Scopus search over 2018 to that date returned 3,701 records on children's reading comprehension, 6,592 on computational text features and 133,132 on platform log data. The pairwise intersections were 17, 28 and 45 records, and the three-way intersection was empty. That count sizes one database under one set of expressions, and it did not return the log analysis of this platform described below, published two months before the search, so the empty cell shows that the intersection is thin and unevenly indexed, not that it is unoccupied. The script that issues these searches and archives their counts is deposited with this protocol [@bernabeuScopusflow2026], @fig-gap shows the sets, and Supplementary Section S4 records the search expressions and the surrounding publication trend. Over the same window, records combining children's reading with machine-generated text went from none before 2024 to two in 2024, six in 2025 and four in the first eight months of 2026. That strand consists of classroom experiments that report gains in comprehension and motivation but describe the texts only qualitatively [@balantekinImprovingStudentsReading2026; @bulutImpactAISTEMBased2026]. Generated and human-written texts have been compared directly, though not yet in children reading for themselves. Generated stories carried fewer personal pronouns and more positive emotion than 100 human-written ones, and adult readers were less transported by them [@appelChatGPTLinguisticProperties2025]. The models tested for children's stories could not hold their vocabulary to a level appropriate for younger readers [@valentiniAutomaticGenerationSimplification2023], which bears on the lexical component directly.

*Let's Story*, a feature of the *Applaydu* app developed by Gameloft and Ferrero International, combines the three topics of that count. Families choose a setting, a hero, a companion, a plot and a theme for each generated story, a generative model writes a narrative around those choices, and the app renders it as an illustrated storybook and, at the family's option, reads it aloud [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025], and every completed reading is logged. Comparable platforms have been studied one feature at a time. @bootonImpactMobileApplication2023 reviewed 11 studies and found inbuilt narration to aid comprehension and word learning. Log data from a research-oriented platform track ability, with reading speed in the BookBites app correlating with standardised scores at *r* = .39 to .48 [@sortkaerBothSidesStory2021]. The commercial edutainment sector, whose user base is far larger, is described in the located literature mainly by content analyses and small experiments [@furlongFindingNeedleHaystack2025; @chatzopoulosEvaluationGooglePlay2023]. One analysis of logs from *Let's Story* itself has appeared. Over 419,700 story sessions in 18 languages across the thirty days following the feature's launch in November 2024, @ratnerProductiveStruggleChildrens2026 describe how children of 4 to 9 meet challenge, reporting completion, where in a story a session was abandoned, and the post-reading difficulty rating. That study is descriptive by design and drawn from aggregated dashboard counts, so its authors state that it cannot follow an individual reader. It leaves every association registered here untested, since no reading time is modelled and the session-level structure a within-child term requires was not in the summaries it drew on. Its window is the first month after launch, where the window analysed here opens more than a year later, so the novelty effects its authors name apply much less to this study. What it does establish is that the difficulty rating, the completion gate and the session record are analysable at scale on this platform.

A machine-checkable theory object deposited with this protocol holds the theoretical commitments behind the hypotheses. It names twelve constructs, eighteen propositions each carrying the mechanism it claims, six auxiliary assumptions and six rival accounts, and records the proposition each prediction derives from and the rival it is meant to separate. The object claims that the time a child spends per word is set by the costs a text imposes at the word, the sentence and the passage. Those costs are discounted by three reader capacities that these data do not measure and for which the age band stands in, and a spoken rendition bears on the first of them more than on the third. Five further propositions carry the same constructs to the quality of the mental model a child ends with. @fig-net, generated from the object, draws them, and they are tested only under the contingent hypotheses, if comprehension items prove to exist. The object passes all twelve items of the versioned rigour checklist implemented in theoryforge, scoring 90.7 out of 100 (Supplementary Section S1) [@bernabeuTheoryforge2026]. Its causal graph is acyclic, so implications can be derived from it mechanically: that the three text properties are mutually independent given the reading level and the generation route, that narration is unrelated to accumulated reading, and that the difficulty rating adds nothing about reading level once reading time is known. We will test these implications before interpreting the confirmatory models, against the criterion registered under Outcome-neutral quality checks, and report any failure.

This study is observational throughout. Children choose their stories, their reading level and whether to switch narration on, and families choose whether to keep using the app. A laboratory experiment establishes that a text property *can* move reading when an experimenter controls the text, the setting and the task, not that it *does* when nobody controls anything. That second question is one about generalisation, and it cannot be settled in the setting that produced the original result [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022; @nastaseKeepItReal2020], so whether a relation holds in a new population of texts, languages and readers is a test of the account that predicts it [@haeffelTestsGeneralizabilityCan2022]. In the logs of a vocabulary-learning app, an effect of valence established under laboratory control held, while an effect of concreteness did not [@wildWordLearningWild2024], though those readers were adults and the outcome was learning. A laboratory result need not survive the move to platform data, and Hypothesis 1 is written so that it need not.

The platform offers three gains in return for that loss of control. The first is stimulus sampling. Reading research has known since Clark [-@clarkLanguageasfixedeffectFallacy1973] that treating a handful of experimenter-written texts as a fixed set inflates confidence in conclusions meant to hold for texts in general, and the mixed-model solution has been available for over a decade [@juddTreatingStimuliRandom2012]. The design here treats Text as a crossed random factor over hundreds of texts that children selected for themselves, which is both the prescribed remedy and, in Brunswik's sense, a representative design [@dhamiRoleRepresentativeDesign2004]. A varying intercept does not by itself make an inference general where the variation between texts is systematic [@bearRandomEffectsWont2022], so the systematic sources the platform records are carried by the model itself. Because an average taken over texts can also hide the variation between them [@simonsohnStimulusSamplingReimagined2025], the text-level deviations will be displayed against the component scores at Stage 2. We avoid the phrase *ecological validity*, which is used in at least two distinct senses, Brunswik's and Orne's [@kihlstromEcologicalValidityEcological2021], and has been argued to be too ill-defined to bear on generalisation at all [@hollemanRealWorldApproachIts2020]. We make the narrower, checkable claim about how the stimuli were sampled.

The second gain is linguistic breadth. English dominates cognitive science to a degree that warps which mechanisms are studied and licenses overgeneralisation from one atypical language to the species [@blasiOverrelianceEnglishHinders2022]. Reading is among the worst affected, because writing systems differ in ways that matter for every stage of processing. The most ambitious response to date, the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus, assembled eye-tracking during text reading in 13 languages, since extended to 21 [@siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022; @siegelmanWave2Multilingual2025], and its authors report that the existing empirical base is insufficient for cross-linguistic comparison. A commercial platform reaches many of the same languages incidentally, in far larger numbers of readers per language, and reaches children where the corpus records skilled adults. It records only whole-story duration where the corpus records eye movements, so the platform gains breadth and loses resolution. The direction of each of the three associations is expected in every one of these ten languages. The operations reading recruits, mapping a written form to sound and to meaning and relating it to what came before, are common to writing systems that differ in almost everything else [@frostUniversalModelReading2012; @verhoevenUniversalsLearningRead2022], and the adult evidence bears this out for word length and frequency across twelve alphabetic languages [@kupermanWordLengthFrequency2024a]. Magnitude is another matter. The lexical association is expected to vary with how a script encodes the word and the grammatical association with a language's word order and statistics, while no comparable reason has been derived for referential continuity, which operates above the word. The language-varying component slopes are where these expectations are visible, they are reported for every language, and no verdict in @tbl-design rests on any one of them.

The third gain is behaviour as it occurred. Logged and self-reported digital media use diverge systematically enough to have warranted a meta-analysis of the discrepancy [@parrySystematicReviewMetaanalysis2021], and in 109 French primary-school children parents' estimates of weekly reading time were three times the logged figure, which predicted fluency better [@brossetteMeasuringReadingTime2026].

Against these gains stands the strongest statistical objection to any large non-random dataset. Meng's [-@mengStatisticalParadisesParadoxes2018] decomposition shows that the error of a sample mean is the product of three quantities: data quality, data quantity and the difficulty of the problem. The first is the correlation between the recorded value and whether it was recorded at all, and probability sampling holds it near zero. Once it is not held there, the population size stops cancelling, and for any given sample size estimation error grows with the square root of the population. Bradley and colleagues [-@bradleyUnrepresentativeBigSurveys2021] gave the canonical demonstration. Two surveys collecting roughly 250,000 responses a week and 75,000 a fortnight overestimated United States COVID-19 vaccine uptake by 17 and 14 percentage points, with margins of error so small that the wrong answers looked precise, while a well-designed panel of about 1,000 responses a week was accurate. Every selection gate in this study is a candidate for that correlation: who owns a tablet, who installs an app tied to a confectionery brand, who registers consent for research use, who switches narration off, and who finishes a story.

That objection has a boundary. Meng's result concerns the estimation of a population mean, and this study estimates no population mean. Its estimands are conditional associations inside the sample, within a language and within a reading level. A gate that operates on the reader alone, such as who owns a tablet or who registers consent, changes which children a slope describes while leaving the slope itself intact. Where the reader attribute also moderates the slope, the estimate becomes the average slope across the families who use the platform, which is how an estimate of a heterogeneous association from a non-random sample should be read [@bryanBehaviouralScienceUnlikely2021]. A slope is distorted only when the gate is a common effect of the text property, or of something that moves with it, and of the outcome or of an unmeasured cause of the outcome, a narrower condition than the one that wrecks a mean [@hernanStructuralApproachSelection2004; @elwertEndogenousSelectionBias2014; @lampCorrectingColliderEffects2025]. Of the gates listed above, only completion meets it, and it is treated next. Narration is a state the models condition on, so the selection it carries falls on the denominators of Hypothesis 4, where it is treated. We will report these coefficients as estimates for children who read on this platform, never as population values for children in general, and we will report no population mean of reading speed for any group.

The extract contains completed readings only, so the analysis conditions on completion, which is plausibly a common effect of the text's difficulty and the reader's capacity. Conditioning on a common effect can induce an association between its causes where none existed [@rohrerThinkingClearlyCorrelations2018], and the direction here is predictable. If harder texts are abandoned more often, the hard texts that survive into the data are disproportionately those read by children who could manage them, which attenuates the very coefficients Hypothesis 1 predicts. If younger children abandon demanding texts more often, their surviving readings of such texts are the more selected and their slopes the more attenuated, which on the sign convention given below pushes the grammatical interaction positive, towards the bottleneck-release account, and the continuity interaction negative, towards the cue-utilisation account [@elwertEndogenousSelectionBias2014; @hernanSelectionBiasDue2023]. The bias therefore works against our own predictions, so a non-negligible result survives the objection more comfortably than a null does. We will report the completion rate by age band, where the data controller can supply it, beside every verdict on Hypotheses 1 to 3, and where the younger band's rate is the lower, a verdict supporting the bottleneck-release or cue-utilisation account will be reported as consistent also with differential attrition.

Abandoning a text is not the only way of escaping it, since a reader can also meet a demanding text by reading it less carefully. Where reading speed was manipulated, comprehension held across a broad band of rates and fell only at the fastest, around 405 words per minute, while the influence of word properties on eye movements persisted throughout [@schwalmTestingSpeedaccuracyTradeoff2026]. That result cuts two ways here. It places the plausibility bound of 400 words per minute close to the rate at which comprehension did give way, so the bound removes page-flipping while leaving fast but still comprehending reading inside the sample. It also gives no warrant for assuming that the faster readings carry weaker text effects, since the word-level effects in that study did not weaken with speed. Neither the extract nor the design can separate a skimmed reading from a fluent one, so we register the ambiguity and no direction for it.

Nothing here is randomised, and we do not use causal verbs for variables that families chose. That restraint is not the same as pretending the questions are not causal, since euphemism has been argued to damage observational research by obscuring what is being asked [@hernanCWordScientificEuphemisms2018; @groszTabooAgainstExplicit2020]. We state the causal structure explicitly in a deposited graph, derive the adjustment set from it, register the rival explanations it implies, and then report associations conditional on that adjustment.

Secondary data also invite the analytic flexibility that preregistration exists to remove, and the field has standards for preregistering analyses of existing data [@westonRecommendationsIncreasingTransparency2019; @vandenakkerPreregistrationSecondaryData2021]. The arrangement described under Data provenance goes further: the data controller holds the extract, unanalysed, and it reaches us only after in-principle acceptance, so the most common objection to observational work, that the analyst saw the data before choosing the analysis, does not arise. Holding the outcome out of reach until the analysis is fixed is the principle of blind analysis [@maccounBlindAnalysisHide2015; @dutilhFlexibleYetFair2021].

This study does not attempt to predict a child's reading. It estimates a handful of pre-specified associations whose attainable precision we calculated before the data were released, and says in advance which of them the available records cannot settle. Group-level associations need not describe any individual, since variance around an expected value was two to four times larger within people than within groups [@fisherLackGrouptoindividualGeneralizability2018]. Tier 2 therefore separates each child's own change from the differences between children, and the two are never reported as a single quantity.

Three consequences of all this are built into the design. First, the reading level a family sets determines which version of a text the platform serves, so text difficulty is partly assigned by a choice that also reflects the child's capacity. We will therefore estimate the text coefficients within reading level and check whether they survive that restriction. Second, the app records elapsed time for a whole story and never for a page, so the outcome is a rate, and we state below which analyses that forecloses. Third, the data carry no measure of any individual child's reading skill, vocabulary or language background, so age band stands in for a bundle of developing capacities and is interpreted as nothing finer. The reading language a family selects need not be the child's first language, so every coefficient below averages over children reading in a first and in a second language. In adult bilinguals reading paragraphs, frequency effects were larger in the second language than in the first and grew as second-language exposure fell [@whitfordSecondlanguageExperienceModulates2012]. A reading language is therefore not a language background, and the country-by-language analysis registered under Sensitivity analyses is the only purchase the extract gives on this.

Under the simple view, reading comprehension is the product of decoding and language comprehension, and decoding's share of the variance falls across the primary grades [@goughDecodingReadingReading1986; @hooverSimpleViewReading1990; @loniganExaminingSimpleView2018]. Automaticity theory says why. Identification that runs without deliberate attention releases capacity for the work of integration [@labergeTowardTheoryAutomatic1974; @perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007], and the reading systems framework separates word identification, word-to-text integration and the situation model [@perfettiWordKnowledgeTheory2014], which is the partition the three components are built to instantiate. Phonological recoding on each new word is the mechanism by which reading itself produces that automaticity [@sharePhonologicalRecodingSelfteaching1995], which ties Hypothesis 6 to the same account. In the eye-movement record, reading efficiency rose by 36 per cent between second and fourth grade in a longitudinal sample, where linguistic skill determined the change and oculomotor skill did not [@huesteggeOculomotorLinguisticDeterminants2009]. In 194 Greek-speaking children, silent reading speed rose from 111 words per minute in grade 3 to 166 in grade 6, through fewer and shorter fixations and longer saccades, and those oculomotor parameters explained variance in speed beyond vocabulary and cognitive measures [@gleniContributionEyeMovements2026]. The age band is therefore read as a coarse proxy for reading experience and the automaticity it confers, in the aggregate and never for one capacity.

The boundary is not ours to set, since the two age bands available to us fall at 7 to 8 and 9 or older. The platform describes its audience as children of 4 to 9 [@ratnerProductiveStruggleChildrens2026], so the older band is expected to sit mostly at its lower edge, and its upper edge is not recorded. Whether change across such a boundary is governed by attained reading level or by the maturation of oculomotor control is still argued [@justinoEyeMovementsDuring2023; @louwenEyeMovementsNatural2026], and the finer-age sensitivity analysis registered below is what these data allow on the question. The LexicalDifficulty × AgeBand interaction is estimated in the tier-1 model and reported, but it carries no registered test and no signed expectation. The eye-movement literature establishes larger absolute lexical effects in children [@tiffin-richardsWordLengthFrequency2015] without settling whether they are larger as a proportion of a slower baseline, the quantity a log outcome measures. The developmental evidence is expressed in raw latencies on isolated words: across grades 2 to 4, word length and regularity effects declined while frequency effects persisted [@hessSublexicalLexicalProcessing2026], and in Italian children of grades 1 to 3 sensitivity to word length fell with age [@zoccolottiWordLengthEffect2005], in a study that manipulated length alone.

The quantity these hypotheses share is the time a child spends per word over a whole story. In the laboratory, reading time carries information about processing because a word is looked at for about as long as it is being worked on [@justTheoryReadingEye1980]. The properties that lengthen fixations also predict passage-level eye-movement measures on texts of more than two hundred words, shown so far in second-language readers of English [@nahatameRevisitingTextReadability2025]. The theory object records that step as the auxiliary assumption that elapsed time indexes effort, on which six of its ten predictions depend, and the positive control on the timing column registered under Outcome-neutral quality checks puts it at risk. A whole-text rate is also more than the sum of its word-level costs, since the efficiency of processing items in a series explained variance in reading connected text once discrete word reading was controlled [@romeroBeyondWordRecognition2024]. The components in this design are properties of the text, so reader-side efficiency sits in the age band and in the residual. We describe the outcome as reading pace, an index of the processing demand a text imposes, and never as a measure of comprehension or fluency, because nothing in these data licenses that reading.

One rival reading of that same interval is registered in the theory object. It traces time on a story to how engaging the story is, where this study traces it to how demanding the text is. Among 122 sixth-graders reading silently, the difficulty of the passage, rated situational interest and their interaction all predicted time on task, and interest accounted for the most variance [@wellandEffectsReadingInstructional2025]. Two registered predictions are marked diagnostic against it. The first is a continuity coefficient non-negligible in the positive direction, which is what an engagement reading would produce, since a text that states more of its connections might hold a child longer where the theory predicts it should release them sooner. The second is Hypothesis 5, since a difficulty rating formed from effort the child noticed expending should rank the three components as reading time does, where a rating tracking enjoyment need not. Neither prediction disposes of the rival on its own.

Six confirmatory hypotheses follow. Two of them, the interactions between the text properties and the age band, are registered as two-sided tests that adjudicate between rival accounts, because the direct developmental evidence in this age range supports neither sign. LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad are oriented so that higher scores mean a more demanding text, and ReferentialContinuity so that higher scores mean a text that states more of the links between its ideas, and signs are fixed before any component score is joined to an outcome. The age band and narration enter the models as deviations from their observed prevalence: a reading scores 1 for the older band, or for narration on, and 0 otherwise, minus the proportion of tier-1 readings in that state. Each component's main effect is then its prevalence-weighted average slope across the two states, which carries no design effect from imbalance, and each interaction is the difference in slope between the two states, positive when the slope is larger in the older band or under narration. The outcome for Hypotheses 1 to 4 and 6 is log reading time per word, standardised within language, so a coefficient is a within-language standardised slope and the region of practical equivalence is 0.05 standard deviations. Hypothesis 4 concerns a difference between two attenuation proportions, with a region of 0.05 on that difference, and Hypothesis 5 uses the child's own three-point difficulty rating on an ordinal scale, where the region is a half-width of log(1.05) on the log-odds scale, an odds ratio between 0.952 and 1.05.

Because the two main effects run in opposite directions, the same developmental claim takes opposite signs in the two interaction terms. Grammatical load is associated with slower reading, so a weaker association in older children makes a positive slope smaller and the interaction negative. Referential continuity is associated with faster reading, so a weaker association in older children makes a negative slope less negative and the interaction positive.

The outcome is the logarithm of reading time. Children in the two age bands differ in overall reading rate, and a difference in rate that is purely multiplicative manufactures a spurious interaction on a raw time scale [@faustIndividualDifferencesInformation1999]. On the log scale, a multiplicative difference in rate appears as a main effect and never as an interaction, so every interaction reported here is a difference in *proportional* cost.

Two things the log scale does not fix are registered here in advance. The first is that the transformation does not remove an interaction produced by an additive component of the interval. If the time a word costs is a base decoding time plus a grammatical increment, the log-scale grammatical slope is that increment divided by the base, so a reader with a smaller base shows a larger proportional slope even where the increment is identical. The automaticity account asserts an additive decoding component of just this kind, so a positive Hypothesis 2 interaction is that account's expected signature on this scale, and the transformation does not manufacture it. The second is that part of any whole-story interval is spent on the illustrations, on turning pages and away from the task. Children's attention to the text of an illustrated book rises across the primary grades [@roycharlandEyeMovementsShared2007], so that non-reading share may be larger in the younger band, making that band's proportional slopes smaller, which moves the Hypothesis 2 interaction towards the positive sign and the Hypothesis 3 interaction towards the negative one. These data cannot separate a smaller base interval that is faster decoding from one that is less time away from the text, so a determinate verdict of either sign will be reported with that limit stated beside it.

The outcome is also divided by word count, and that choice has a rationale and a residue of its own. In the standard cohesion manipulation, the more cohesive version of a text is 20 to 40 per cent longer, so a duration aggregated over a whole text would show higher cohesion slowing reading for arithmetic reasons alone. Dividing by word count and retaining log text length as a covariate closes that path, and a raw duration is never used as an outcome. Dividing by words does not divide out sentence boundaries, at which readers spend extra time whose cause is unsettled [@raynerEffectClauseWrapup2000; @warrenInvestigatingCausesWrapup2009], so a text of shorter sentences carries more boundaries per word. That works against the expected sign of sentence length taken alone.

@tbl-design sets out each hypothesis against the sampling and analysis plan that tests it, the precision the design analysis says that test requires, how each possible outcome will be read, and what would be shown wrong. We fixed every row before any outcome data existed.
