*Hypothesis 1: text properties and reading pace.* We predict that, across distinct texts and within reading level and language, LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad will each show a positive association with log reading time per word, and ReferentialContinuity a negative one. The three coefficients are evaluated and labelled separately under the readings in @tbl-design, and the failure of one does not suppress reporting of the others. Two of those readings need a rationale. A positive continuity coefficient is not labelled a reverse cohesion effect, because that effect is a learning outcome [@mcnamaraAreGoodTexts1996; @mcnamaraLearningTextsEffects1996; @oreillyReversingCohesionEffect2007] which on the construction-integration account arises where a less cohesive text makes the knowledgeable reader infer more, and on a time scale that would appear as slower reading of the less cohesive text. A grammatical coefficient practically equivalent to zero would extend to children the negligible passage-level effect of global complexity measures reported for adults [@kupermanGlobalMeasuresSyntactic2025], a reading that does not carry over to the lexical component, whose anchors are word-level aggregates the adult study did not test at passage level.

One further rule follows from how narration is distributed. Narration was on in about nine sessions in ten of the structural sample, so each prevalence-weighted main effect is dominated by the narrated slope. If the recording sets the pace of narrated sessions, the continuity slope under narration converges on zero and the lexical slope on the recording's own duration function, as set out under Hypothesis 4. Where the compression diagnostic registered under Confirmatory models fires, the derived unnarrated slope therefore carries a component's Hypothesis 1 verdict whenever the distinct texts carrying unnarrated readings number at least that component's threshold, with the prevalence-weighted slope reported beside it. That threshold is re-derived from the deposited texts sweep at the observed number of unnarrated readings per text, as the seventh adjustment registered under Design and precision analysis. Where the unnarrated texts fall short of it, the prevalence-weighted verdict stands and is reported beside the unnarrated slope, and an inside-region continuity verdict or a non-negligible lexical verdict is then reported as consistent with the recording having set the pace. The rule is fixed here and does not depend on the sign of any coefficient.

*Hypothesis 2: grammatical load and the age band.* We register the GrammaticalLoad × AgeBand interaction as a two-sided adjudicating test, because accounts of what changes between these ages divide over the sign on the scale this study uses. On the capacity account, a grammatical dependency costs time in proportion to how close its maintenance comes to exhausting the working memory available, so as that capacity matures the same structure costs proportionally less and the interaction is negative [@justCapacityTheoryComprehension1992; @kingIndividualDifferencesSyntactic1991]. Working-memory span does track complex-syntax comprehension and production between the ages of 5 and 12 [@delageSyntaxWorkingMemory2019]. The experience-based alternative to capacity shares that sign, since on it what grows with age is exposure to complex structure, and exposure makes the structure cheaper [@macdonaldReassessingWorkingMemory2002]. That children with more print exposure produce relative clauses more as adults do [@montagInfluenceLanguageStatistics2015] is evidence about production, not about the cost of reading such a structure. The account that predicts the opposite sign holds that what changes is the base the proportion is taken over, and how fully structure is built on it. The time a word costs carries a decoding component alongside the cost of grammatical load, and as print-to-sound mapping automatises that component shrinks [@labergeTowardTheoryAutomatic1974], leaving the reader with representations whose quality makes retrieval cheap [@perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007], so an unchanged absolute grammatical cost occupies a larger proportion of a smaller base and the interaction is positive. Comprehenders often leave syntactic structure shallow or unresolved, structure left unresolved is read faster, and the evidence for that claim is mixed [@ferreiraGoodEnoughRepresentations2002; @swetsUnderspecificationSyntacticAmbiguities2008; @francesGoodEnoughProcessing2024]. Children of 8 to 10 show the same signatures as adults, and the older children among them attend more to the punctuation that marks clause boundaries [@wonnacottChildrensReadingGood2016], so a younger reader who builds shallower structure incurs less of a dependency's cost. The capacity account is the theory object's own proposition and the bottleneck-release account is registered there as its rival, so a positive interaction would count against that proposition as well as for the rival.

The capacity account's premise is less secure in this age range than its formulation suggests. Across 197 studies, the relation between working memory and reading was moderate, *r* = .29, and its contribution to comprehension was accounted for by decoding and vocabulary where those were controlled [@pengExaminingMediationEffects2018]. In children, memory span has been related to relative-clause comprehension, though narrowly in both studies located: in German-speaking 7-year-olds the relation was to digit span and held for object relatives alone [@arosioMorphologicalInformationMemory2012], and in French- and German-speaking children verbal working memory correlated with object-relative comprehension only in French [@solaimaniBilingualismWorkingMemory2025]. The premise may therefore not hold uniformly across the languages in this sample, which is one reason this interaction is also reported separately by language.

The direct evidence does not decide between the accounts. The largest eye-movement sample over this band, 81 children reading 12 items, found no attenuation [@wonnacottChildrensReadingGood2016]. It manipulated temporary ambiguity, which indexes reanalysis, a different demand from the sustained maintenance that dependency length imposes, so its null does not transfer to the present operationalisation. Where an interaction has been reported, it was confined to late measures with fourteen children per group [@josephChildrensAdultsOnline2013]. Recomputed from that study's tables as a proportion of baseline, the two measures disagree. On go-past time in the target region, our computation gives 15 per cent in the younger children, 25 per cent in the older and 31 per cent in adults, which is the pattern a positive interaction would reproduce on a proportional scale. On post-target total reading time, where the study's own significant interaction lay, the proportional effect ran the other way, from 27 per cent in the younger children to 12 per cent in the older and 4.5 per cent in adults.

A third possibility is that development over this band is not monotonic at all. The largest of the existing tests, with 250 children aged 8 to 11 reading and hearing sentences word by word, reported a U-shaped pattern in the online processing of restrictive relative clauses over that range [@boothDevelopmentRelativeClause2000]. Offline comprehension of complex syntax grows most steeply between 5;6 and 7 years [@frizelleDevelopmentRelativeClause2025], so the younger band sits immediately after the steepest phase. The boundary between the bands also coincides with a documented shift in online processing. In Russian-speaking children, accuracy on passive sentences rose sharply between 7 and 8, and although 8- to 10-year-olds then matched adults on accuracy, the incremental-revision signature at the critical word, present in adults and at 8 to 10, was absent at 6 to 7 [@kruchininaEyemovementSignaturesSyntactic2026]. Accuracy converged before processing did, and a time-based outcome is the grain at which that difference shows.

The three outcomes are read as @tbl-design states. Two patterns would produce an inside-region posterior without showing that no developmental signature exists, a non-monotonic trajectory cancelling across two coarse bands and interactions of opposite sign in orthographies of different depth, so the per-language interactions and the finer-age sensitivity analysis registered below are reported beside the pooled coefficient.

The two interactions are coupled under bottleneck release. The same dilution that raises the proportional grammatical cost in the older band deepens the proportional continuity saving. Bottleneck release therefore predicts a positive Hypothesis 2 interaction, a negative Hypothesis 3 one and a lexical-by-age interaction that is negative or null. The tier-1 model already estimates all three, and we will report the joint pattern descriptively beside the two registered coefficients, where it gates no verdict.

*Hypothesis 3: referential continuity and the age band.* We register the ReferentialContinuity × AgeBand interaction the same way, because the construction-integration account of comprehension [@kintschRoleKnowledgeDiscourse1988], set beside what exploiting a cohesive cue requires, supplies two moderators of coherence facilitation, both rising between 7 and 11 and pushing in opposite directions. On the knowledge account, a gap in the text is bridged from knowledge that the younger reader has less of and retrieves less readily. Age differences in coherence inferencing between 6 and 15 survived making the relevant knowledge equally available to every child, and its accessibility mattered more for the younger children [@barnesEffectsKnowledgeAvailability1996]. At 11 to 12, higher knowledge went with faster reading of sentences that required an inference [@cainInfluenceReaderText2024]. Surface continuity substitutes for an inference that is costlier at 7 to 8 than at 9 and over, so it is worth most to the younger reader and the interaction is positive.

On the cue-utilisation account, exploiting a connective requires enough decoding fluency to reach it and enough explicit knowledge of what it signals, so the older reader gains more and the interaction is negative. Knowledge of causal and adversative conjunctions is still developing between 8 and 10 [@cainAgeAbilityrelatedDifferences2005; @cainInfluenceConnectivesYoung2011], and comprehension of connectives grows across the primary years [@volodinaComprehensionConnectivesDevelopment2020]. The cue-utilisation account runs through decoding fluency, so it implies a larger negative interaction where decoding is still maturing across the two bands, which the paragraph on orthographic depth below places in English, French and Portuguese. The knowledge account, which runs through background knowledge and narrative experience, implies no such dependence. The per-language interactions registered under Sensitivity analyses are reported for that reason as well, and they are descriptive, gating no verdict on Hypothesis 3.

Decoding fluency and knowledge of the cue both develop well past the ages studied here. Knowledge of what a connective signals is still incomplete in French-speaking teenagers of 12 to 19 and in native Russian-speaking teenagers of 11 to 17, and in both samples vocabulary size and exposure to print were stronger correlates of appropriate use than age was [@tskhovrebovaFrenchspeakingTeenagersMastery2022; @tskhovrebovaVocabularySizeExposure2023]. Both moderators, background knowledge and knowledge of the cue, are themselves likely to grow with the reading a child accumulates, which is a further reason the net sign of the interaction is not derivable in advance. The knowledge account is likewise the theory object's own proposition, and cue utilisation is registered there as its rival, so a negative interaction counts against that proposition.

The inference the knowledge account has continuity sparing is the one that referential overlap and semantic similarity between adjacent sentences make unnecessary, whereas the cue-utilisation account concerns a connective. Semantic and causal relatedness dissociate by reader skill in adults, semantic relatedness weighing more for the less skilled reader [@todaroImpactSemanticCausal2010], and the two bear differently on processing time and on what is remembered [@wolfeCausalSemanticRelatedness2005]. The three anchors of ReferentialContinuity need not therefore carry the same age interaction, and a component interaction inside the region could arise from anchors whose interactions differ in sign. The per-anchor check registered under Sensitivity analyses does not gate the verdict. Where the component posterior lies inside the region while the anchor interactions lie outside it with opposite signs, the equivalence verdict stands and is reported with that pattern beside it.

A negative interaction has a second reading. On the Landscape model, whether a reader attempts a bridging inference depends on the standard of coherence they bring to the text [@vandenbroekCognitiveProcessesDiscourse2017; @vandenbroekIntegratingMemorybasedConstructionist2005]. A reader who does not attempt it pays no time for the gap, so continuity would save the younger reader nothing if that band read to a lower standard. The online evidence bounds that concern. Children of 8 to 13 made the local inferences a coherent representation required, if not the optional ones [@josephOnlineInferenceMaking2021]. Among the accounts on which continuity is worth more to the older reader, cue utilisation and a lower standard of coherence are not separated by this design, and a negative verdict is reported as consistent with both.

Here too the existing evidence does not decide between the accounts. Eight- and ten-year-olds gained the same speed-up from an appropriate connective in self-paced reading, with the age interaction explicitly null across 91 children [@cainInfluenceConnectivesYoung2011]. No difference in online sensitivity to a coherence break was found between children of 8 to 9 and children of 10 to 11 [@helderCoherenceMonitoringGood2016]. Among 8- to 10-year-olds reading two-clause sentences, the absence of the Dutch causal connective lengthened processing only for second-language readers with weaker syntactic knowledge [@vandenboschOnlineProcessingCausal2018], a contrast between language backgrounds that leaves age untested, in which the connective was worth most to the reader with least resource. In fourth-graders, the effect of cohesion turned on world knowledge and far less on decoding skill, with age untestable within a single grade [@mcnamaraComprehensionChallengesFourth2011]. In the studies located for this age range, the outcome measured under a whole-text coherence manipulation is comprehension or inference, so none of them bears directly on reading rate. The three outcomes are read as for Hypothesis 2. Because the sign of a coherence effect also depends on which cohesive device carries it, connectives enter by relation type and the component's anchors are the causal and contrastive connectives. The facilitation a connective affords was smaller for result relations than for concessive ones and differed between an analytic and a synthetic language [@marchalFacilitatingEffectConnectives2025], which supports both halves of that decision.

Both age-band interactions are averaged over ten languages whose orthographies differ in depth, and the band does not mean the same thing in all of them. Children in most European orthographies read familiar words accurately and fluently before the end of the first school year, while the rate of development in English is more than twice as slow, with French and Portuguese also lagging [@seymourFoundationLiteracyAcquisition2003]. Psycholinguistic grain size theory derives that pattern from how consistently a writing system represents phonology, which sets the size of the units a learner comes to rely on [@zieglerReadingAcquisitionDevelopmental2005]. Children matched on years of instruction show orthography-specific length and frequency signatures, English qualitatively unlike German and Finnish, while adults converge [@schroederEyeMovementsChildren2022]. Between two transparent orthographies the developmental trajectory can nonetheless be comparable, with language-specific effects confined to morphological complexity [@marziComparableReadingDevelopment2026], so the heterogeneity expected here is a matter of degree. Children reading different orthographies therefore sit at different points on the automatisation curve, and on the bottleneck-release reading the developmental signature would be largest where decoding automatises latest. The registered coefficient is a prevalence-weighted average across those positions, and we do not generalise it from any one orthography [@shareAnglocentricitiesCurrentReading2008].

*Hypothesis 4: the selectivity of narration.* We predict that the LexicalDifficulty coefficient will be proportionally smaller under narration than the ReferentialContinuity coefficient is. Writing $\pi_{\text{lex}}$ and $\pi_{\text{cont}}$ for the proportional attenuation of each coefficient under narration, computed draw by draw from the posterior under the rule given under Confirmatory models, the prediction is that $\pi_{\text{lex}} - \pi_{\text{cont}} > 0.20$. A spoken rendition supplies word identity without print-to-sound mapping, the step that a low-frequency or long word makes expensive, and it does not supply the link between two ideas, which the reader must still construct. A voice also carries prosodic phrasing, which a silent reader must project for themselves [@breenEmpiricalInvestigationsImplicit2014] and which is still developing across the primary years [@goddeReviewReadingProsody2020], so narration could lower the grammatical coefficient by a route unrelated to word identity. Prosodic phrasing does not supply the link between two sentences, though, which keeps the lexical-against-continuity contrast interpretable. The grammatical-by-narration interaction is estimated in the same model, reported for description, and enters no decision rule. The sparing is conditional on timing. In reading while listening, adults' eyes generally ran ahead of the audio and rarely rested on the word being heard [@conklinWhatEyetrackingTells2020], and among 119 learners of English the multimodal condition ran slightly slower than reading alone [@maloneEyeMovementsItem2025], whereas children of 8 to 9 pattern the other way [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. The decoding account therefore describes the reader slower than the recording and the pacing account the reader faster than it, and the full-sample contrast reports which regime dominates the narrated sessions. The benefit of text-to-speech is largest for children whose decoding is weak but whose language is intact [@keelorImpactTexttospeechFeatures2023], and in 34 children aged 8 to 9 the time saved fell on the first encounter with an orthographically novel word and had gone by the second [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024].

The competing account holds that narrated reading time is set by the duration of the recording, in which case each narrated slope converges on the slope of the recording's duration per word. That quantity is near zero for referential continuity and positive for lexical properties tied to word length, since a recording runs longer per word where words carry more syllables. The two attenuations are therefore equal only once the recording's duration is accounted for, and without that adjustment the pacing account predicts $\pi_{\text{lex}} - \pi_{\text{cont}}$ at or below zero. Reading aloud runs at about 183 words per minute against 238 to 260 silent, and the gap between text types is predicted by word length [@brysbaertHowManyWords2019]. Pacing alone also fails to flatten word-level effects, since manipulating reading speed left the influence of word properties on eye movements in place [@schwalmTestingSpeedaccuracyTradeoff2026], which is one reason the registered contrast sets the lexical attenuation against the continuity attenuation. The compression diagnostic withholds the full-sample verdict where the recording sets the pace for most narrated sessions, and an adjustment for the recording's duration covers the mixture that diagnostic can miss. That adjustment rests on a predicted spoken duration per word, computed from the held texts before any outcome is joined and defined under Materials, and the refit that carries it is registered under Sensitivity analyses.

That account has substantial support of its own. The aggregate comprehension benefit of reading while listening is confined to studies whose comparison condition was externally paced [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023]. A registered report testing the resource-freeing mechanism in 86 adult second-language readers found comprehension *worse* under narration than in silent reading, and found that individual differences in orthographic decoding and speech segmentation did not interact with input condition in the way that account predicts [@huiForcedPaceReading2026]. In 21 secondary-school students with dyslexia and 22 without, audio support increased reading time in most tasks while leaving comprehension unchanged [@knoopvancampenEffectAudiosupportStrategy2021]. Where the compression has been measured incidentally it is severe, since the standard deviation of exposure time fell from 11.56 seconds when self-paced to 0.62 seconds when narrated [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. The tests located bear on comprehension outcomes and on the variance of exposure time, not on the contrast Hypothesis 4 registers.

A third possibility shares the pacing account's predictions, that the child listens and does not read, so that the interval is the recording plus the page turns. Attention to print is low in preschoolers listening to a storybook [@evansWhatChildrenAre2005] and rises across the primary grades with reading skill [@roycharlandEyeMovementsShared2007]. In older children reading an illustrated story in a second language, audio moved the eyes from the text to the pictures without changing comprehension [@pellicersanchezYoungLearnersProcessing2020; @serranoYoungL2Learners2022], whereas 8- to 9-year-olds did fixate the words under bimodal presentation [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. The share of narrated sessions that were read along is therefore unknown and is likely to differ by age band. The logs cannot separate a paced reading from a listening, so an inside-region verdict is reported as time set by the recording, whether or not the child read along, and never as evidence that narrated reading was reading. The narrated sessions the audio cannot have paced are the only part of the design that excludes listening by construction.

The four outcomes, their posterior criteria and the reading of each are registered in @tbl-design and under Decision rules. The threshold of 0.20 is four times the region's half-width and is a registered convention. A difference determinately below -0.05, meaning that narration removes more of the continuity cost than of the lexical cost, is consistent either with reverse selectivity, which contradicts both accounts, or with pacing acting through the recording's duration, which lengthens the audio for texts with longer words. The duration-adjusted sensitivity contrast is reported beside it as the quantity that separates the two.

Who reads without narration is itself a selection. Narration was on in about nine sessions in ten of the structural sample, so the unnarrated slopes, which are the denominators of both attenuation proportions, are estimated largely from the families who chose to switch the audio off. If those are disproportionately the fluent readers, their slopes are attenuated by selection and both proportions are distorted, and the data carry no measure of reading skill with which to adjust for this. We will therefore report narration prevalence by age band, reading level and language before fitting, and the rule under Confirmatory models promotes the within-account contrast to the primary estimate where the data allow it. Because the contrast is a ratio, it is evaluated only when the unnarrated slopes of the lexical and continuity components are both practically non-negligible. If either is not, there is no attenuation to compare and Hypothesis 4 is reported as not evaluable, under a gating rule that does not depend on the sign of any coefficient.

*Hypothesis 5: the child's own judgement of difficulty.* We predict that, in an ordinal model of the post-reading rating, LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad will be associated with higher odds of a harder rating and ReferentialContinuity with lower odds, each by an odds ratio outside the region. We further predict that the three standardised coefficients will rank by magnitude as they do in the reading-time model. Two measures of the same three constructs, one behavioural and one judgement-based, obtained on different scales from overlapping sets of children, are not bound to rank those constructs the same way, so agreement on order is a substantive prediction of the effort account, which measuring effort twice would deliver for free.

The link between the two measures rests on the effort heuristic of the cue-utilisation account, on which a judgement of difficulty is inferred from cues, experienced effort among them, and is not a direct reading of processing [@koriatMonitoringOnesOwn1997; @undorfJudgmentsLearningReflect2011]. Two meta-analyses put the association between experienced effort and monitoring judgements at *r* = -.36 and, in a meta-analytic structural model, at $\beta$ = -.19 [@baarsRelationStudentsEffort2020; @davidRelationPerceivedMental2024]. Those judgements are judgements of learning and of confidence, so for a difficulty rating the sign is the mirror image. Second, third and fifth graders were less confident in an answer the longer they had taken to choose it, and reliance on that cue was stronger in the older children [@koriatChoiceLatencyCue2010]. On the proposition the theory object records, the rating is not a second instrument trained on the text but a downstream report of the same expended effort that the reading interval times. Effort is attributed to the material when the material imposes it, and effort a learner chooses to invest carries no such attribution, a distinction established in adult learners [@koriatIntricateRelationshipsMonitoring2006; @koriatJudgmentsLearningDepend2014]. In children, the association duly weakens where regulation is goal driven [@baarsRelationStudentsEffort2020].

Reading in this app is self-paced and voluntary, which is one reason the rating is registered here as a measure under test. It is also why the theory object marks this prediction as diagnostic against the rival on which time on a text indexes how engaging the story was. Convergence in the predicted directions therefore weighs against that rival, and its absence is read under the rule registered in @tbl-design, as a failure of the rating and not as support for the rival.

The cue-utilisation account also supplies a reason the two measures might diverge, because a judgement made after finishing draws on the cues still accessible at that moment and the three sources of demand are not equally accessible. Word-level difficulty recurs at every line, whereas the cost of an unstated link between ideas is spread over the text, and a cohesion manipulation that moved paragraph-level judgements left whole-text judgements untouched unless readers could still consult the text [@lefevreTextCohesionMetacomprehension2004]. The evidence is not one-sided, since in adults predicting their own recall, judgements about a whole text did rise with coherence [@rawsonArePerformancePredictions2002]. The posterior probability that the two measures rank the components alike is the study's principal convergent-validity check, read against the 0.90 criterion registered under Decision rules.

Two facts about the rating constrain the design. The first is that the nearest evidence is adjacent to what this rating asks. Among children of 8 to 10 solving arithmetic problems, the mental effort they reported investing was related to their judgements of their own learning, which tracked the complexity of the problem [@baarsAccuracyPrimarySchool2018]. Children in both of this study's bands judge how well they have understood a text [@steinerDevelopmentChildrensMonitoring2020], fifth graders do so both for the whole text and for individual answers [@markovichMetacognitiveMonitoringReading2026], and primary school children are more overconfident in those judgements than secondary school children are [@mirandolaMetacognitiveMonitoringText2018]. That overconfidence depends on the text: among 407 primary and secondary students, the primary children overestimated their performance on expository passages and inferential questions but calibrated as well as the older students on narrative texts [@zagatoHowSureAm2026], and every text in this study is narrative. Those are judgements about the reader's own comprehension, whereas the rating here asks about the text. In adults, subjective comprehensibility ratings of narrative text can be predicted from computed text features [@tilmatinePredictingSubjectiveRatings2024]. The child metacognition literature located rates adjacent things, and none of it validates a global post-reading judgement of a text's difficulty against the text's measured properties in children of this age. We likewise found no psychometric evaluation of the three-point easy, just right and difficult format, which is a classroom heuristic.

The second is that children's monitoring judgements are internally consistent when aggregated over items, their reliability is bounded by the reliability of the first-order task, and their accuracy varies from one task to another [@roebersExploringPsychometricProperties2021; @eberhartMetacognitiveMonitoringEarly2025]. The design therefore aggregates ratings at text level and applies the five-rater floor. Children of 6 to 13 have a limited grasp of multi-point response formats, word-anchored options agreeing better than numeric ones with a yes-or-no standard [@mellorUseLikertScales2014], and the number of options bears on how reliably children and young adolescents answer, four options proving optimal and seven or more lowering reliability [@borgersResponseEffectsSurveys2004]. Which way any of this would move a three-point difficulty rating inside an app is not established, so we register the direction as unknown and report the observed distribution. The identification of a reported difficulty with expended effort is itself contestable, since in 80 children aged 8 to 12 the difficulty and effort ratings given after a battery of cognitive tasks were uncorrelated with each other and only weakly related to performance [@torresMetacognitiveRatingsCognitive2026].

Judging a task by the effort it cost is itself something children come to do. In self-paced learning, judgements of learning fell as study time rose for third to sixth graders, aged 9 to 12, and showed no such relation for first and second graders, aged 7 and 8 [@koriatMemorizingEffortHeuristic2009], a division that falls on this study's two bands. None of this settles the matter for a direct judgement of a text, since even 5- and 6-year-olds use an item's difficulty adaptively when evaluating their own performance [@vanloonDevelopmentalProgressionPerformance2017], so a rating that tracks the text at 7 to 8 remains possible. The rating model carries the same component-by-age-band terms as the timing model, and we will report the band-specific odds ratios beside the pooled ones as descriptive quantities, the registered tests remaining the pooled odds ratios and the ordering. The recorded bands in the structural sample skewed towards the younger of the two (Supplementary Section S8), so a prevalence-weighted pooled odds ratio will be weighted towards it. That is why @tbl-design reads a pooled odds ratio inside the region, beside an older-band odds ratio outside it, as a limit on the rating specific to the younger band.

The effective sample size is the number of distinct children rating each text, and the raw count of ratings overstates it, so the model carries a text varying intercept, and we will report the distribution of raters per text before fitting, applying the five-rater floor registered under Confirmatory models. We will report the intraclass correlation for the rating at text level, a reliability estimate for this format. We will also report the distribution of the three rating categories overall and by age band and language before fitting, and beside any inside-region verdict, because a distribution concentrated in one category limits what a cumulative logit can resolve.

A failure here is ambiguous on its own, and Hypothesis 1 resolves it, which is why the readings in @tbl-design are conditioned on the reading-time coefficients. Components that predict reading time but not the rating leave the feature pipeline sound and the rating unusable as a measure of experienced difficulty, components that predict neither are themselves suspect, and a mismatch in ordering alone is reported as evidence about which cues children use, leaving the components untouched. This hypothesis is also the one the design analysis marks as most likely to be underpowered. An inconclusive verdict at the census is itself informative, because it bounds the reliability a single-item difficulty check can have at the availability such apps achieve. In that case the ordering is reported descriptively and convergent validity is recorded as not established, so that the fifth outcome-neutral check has a defined outcome whether or not Hypothesis 5 reaches a verdict.

*Hypothesis 6: accumulated reading and pace.* We predict that, among children with several recorded sessions, a one-standard-deviation within-child increase in a child's own accumulated in-app reading, on the log scale on which it is entered, will be associated with a reduction in that child's log reading time per word. The reduction is predicted over and above session order, the interval since the previous session and the time elapsed since the child's first session. The unit is the standard deviation because that is the unit in which the region of practical equivalence is defined under Decision rules, and the implied change per doubling of accumulated words will be reported beside the coefficient.

On the orthographic-learning account, each successful encounter with a written word form is an opportunity to acquire or sharpen the word-specific orthographic representation supporting its later recognition [@sharePhonologicalRecodingSelfteaching1995]. The quality of those representations makes skilled word reading cheap [@perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007], and experience of print is accordingly treated as the engine of growth in word reading [@nationNurturingLexicalLegacy2017; @castlesEndingReadingWars2018; @deaconTestingMechanismsUnderlying2024]. Because the mechanism operates on items, the dose is counted in words of completed distinct stories, and repeated readings are held back for the sensitivity analysis registered below. Because each further form adds less as the lexicon fills, the dose enters on a log scale.

Learning of this kind is in the first place item-based. Children in grades 1 and 2 who met novel spellings in short stories learned them, but transferred that learning clearly only to orthographically related forms [@tuckerEarlySelfteaching2025], and across 62 experiments the outcome is modulated by language-specific word properties [@liSystematicReviewOrthographic2023]. Reading one story can therefore make the next cheaper by two routes, the words the two texts share and the sublexical regularities a reader generalises from them [@castlesEndingReadingWars2018], so how far the association reaches is bounded by how much of a new text earlier reading can already have discounted. Both bounds are looser for stories written to one reading level than for texts sampled at large, and neither is measured here. Grades 1 and 2 sit below this study's bands. Outside English, orthographic learning, lexical knowledge, reading fluency and spelling were associated in German-speaking primary school children [@schmalzDoFasterLearners2025]. The account is not neutral between the ten languages. Decoding automatises at very different ages across them, as the paragraph on orthographic depth above records [@seymourFoundationLiteracyAcquisition2003]. On a model in which decipherability precedes unitisation and automatisation [@shareBlueprintUniversalTheory2025], the per-unit speed-up that accumulated reading affords should therefore be shallower where decoding was automatised earlier. The pooled deviation coefficient remains the registered test, and the per-language slopes from the secondary refit registered under Sensitivity analyses are reported descriptively beside it, annotated with orthographic depth for the eight sampled languages Seymour and colleagues covered, with Polish and Korean reported without an annotation.

The relation between practice and skill is reciprocal over years [@torppaLeisureReadingNot2020; @vanbergenHowArePractice2021], so the coefficient is an association within the observation window, and never an estimate of a practice effect. Random-intercept cross-lagged models on more than 5,100 German secondary students found no within-person evidence that reading more yields better reading competence, while the reverse path, from competence to exposure, remained [@bittmannReadingBegetsReading2025]. Only a design that holds the two apart can show such an asymmetry, and this one holds them apart by construction. On the other arm, exposure to a text experimentally speeded skilled adults' later recognition of the low-frequency words in it [@chetailReadingBooksPositive2024], which is the closest experimental demonstration located, in adults and confined to rare words. That reciprocity has been established at yearly lags, so it does not by itself license treating the reverse path as negligible over a window of months. A child whose session went slowly may not return, so later sessions would be contributed disproportionately by children whose earlier sessions went well, which would push the coefficient in the predicted direction. A child reading faster may also choose longer stories, or a family may raise the reading level, and either change alters the composition of what accumulates even though the current story's length and level are adjusted for. Before the coefficient is interpreted we will report the distribution of each account's final-session pace relative to that account's own mean, and the number of accounts whose reading level changed within the window, which the audit establishes in any case. Two refits will be reported beside the registered term and will gate nothing: one excluding every account's final eligible session, and one adding the previous session's standardised pace as a covariate, in the spirit of the random-intercept cross-lagged model [@hamakerCritiqueCrosslaggedPanel2015]. The second is read with the caveat that conditioning on a lagged outcome alongside an account intercept is itself biased in short series, so it bounds the concern without settling it.

The account-mean term that enters alongside the deviation is reported but is not a test of either account. Both predict it negative, since a child who has read more in the app may read faster for having done so and a child who reads faster may go on reading. How much and how well children read have long been associated at the between-person level [@molReadNotRead2011]. Only the within-child deviation separates the accounts, and the rival has content of its own. In three twin samples, the modelled direction of causation ran from reading ability, literacy skill or comprehension to print exposure or literacy enjoyment, with the reverse influence zero in one sample [@vanbergenWhyChildrenRead2018; @vanbergenLiteracySkillsSeem2023; @erbeliUnravelingRelationReading2020].

Each covariate is there for a named alternative. Session order absorbs familiarity with the interface and with the generator's story schemas, since a reader who knows the shape of a story reads it faster for reasons the orthographic-learning account does not claim. Days since the previous session absorbs spacing. Days since the first session absorbs maturation and schooling. What identifies the accumulated-words deviation once the three are held is within-child variation in the lengths of the stories already read, which is thin where the reading level fixes story length, and that thinness is one reason the tier-2 requirement is re-derived at the observed distribution before fitting. Oral reading fluency grows appreciably and unevenly over a school year [@christCurriculumbasedMeasurementOral2010], so an elapsed-time covariate absorbs maturation only if growth is close to linear in days within a child and the window's position in the school year is immaterial. Growth rates also differ between children, and their predictors [@khanolainenPredictingReadingFluency2024] are among the things that also predict how much a child reads. Before Hypothesis 6 is interpreted we will report the within-child correlation matrix of the four covariates and the deviation term, with their variance inflation factors, and the calendar month of each session as a descriptive stratifier, so that a window spanning a school holiday is visible.

The readings of a negative, a positive and an inside-region posterior are registered in @tbl-design. This hypothesis depends on a subsample whose size is not known before the extract is released, and it is declared underpowered, not untestable, if that subsample falls below the threshold re-derived for it under Design and precision analysis.

Every hypothesis is labelled under the single posterior rule given under Decision rules and diagnostics, and an inconclusive result is reported as such. No hypothesis is filtered by a preliminary significance test. Three labels apply before a verdict. A hypothesis is declared untestable, before its model is fitted and without reference to any coefficient, if its component fails the construction rule set out under the dimension reduction or if its outcome or contrast is absent from the frozen extract. A hypothesis whose data fall below its precision threshold in @tbl-design, as re-derived under Design and precision analysis where that section says so, is instead declared underpowered. Its model is still fitted and reported, and no conclusion is drawn from an interval the design analysis predicted would be indeterminate. A hypothesis is reported as not evaluable when a registered post-fitting contingency removes its test, which happens in two cases only: the Hypothesis 4 gate, and failure of the positive control on the timing column.

The limits of what follows should be equally clear. This study will not identify a causal effect of any text property, age band or narration setting. It will not estimate how fast children in general read, nor generalise beyond families who chose to install and use this application. It will say nothing about comprehension, since none of the contingent hypotheses is activated at submission. The constraints on generality are those stated here: children aged 7 and over who read narrative texts of a few hundred words on a touchscreen, in one of ten languages, inside one commercial application whose texts one generator produced [@simonsConstraintsGeneralityCOG2017]. The medium is part of that boundary, and it is not neutral. Reading on screen yields poorer comprehension than reading the same text on paper, with the shortfall larger under time pressure and for informational text [@delgadoDontThrowAway2018], and in children the paper advantage holds except where a digital text adds features aligned with the content [@furenesComparisonChildrensReading2021]. A network meta-analysis of 56 samples locates most of that shortfall in scrolling: where scrolling was required, paper beat every device by 0.35 to 0.48 standard deviations, and where it was not, the differences ran from 0.03 to 0.12 and were unreliable, with a tablet read without scrolling ranked closest to paper [@clintonlisellDecodingDigitalReading2026]. This app serves a story as pages on a tablet, so the largest known moderator of the screen shortfall does not apply here. The laboratory results the three components are built on were obtained largely on paper, so the comparison drawn here is across media as well as across settings, and a coefficient smaller than its laboratory counterpart has that second explanation available alongside the first. Where the data controller's answers falsify an auxiliary assumption, the affected predictions are reassigned by the rules in @tbl-unresolved, never reinterpreted after the fact.
